summary: Updates RFC 8138 by defining a bit in the RPL DODAG Configuration option that says whether compression is used in the RPL Instance, and specifies how nodes compliant with RFC 8138 behave when the bit is set or unset.

eli5.summary: A flag that tells all devices whether the shortened packet headers are in use, so they all handle packets the same way.

subtitle: A single flag in RPL's configuration message that tells a low-power network when it is safe to switch on compressed routing headers.

tldr.problem: Turning on the 6LoWPAN routing header compression of RFC 8138 in a running low-power network normally needs a flag day, because nodes that do not support it would fail to communicate or drop compressed packets.
tldr.mechanism: A new 'T' flag in the RPL DODAG Configuration option, set only by the Root and copied unchanged down the DODAG, says whether compression is in use. Nodes generate compressed packets if and only if the flag is set.
tldr.outcome: A live network can be migrated with compression left off until every node is upgraded, then switched on globally. This RFC updates RFC 8138 and is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Flag position
facts.value: Bit 2 of the reserved flags, counting from bit 0 as the most significant

today: RFC 9035 is a Proposed Standard from April 2021 and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 8138, so the two are read together.

sections.title: The Migration Problem
sections.content:
Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs) are designed mainly to save energy. The routing optimizations in RPL (RFC 6550), such as routing along a DODAG (Destination-Oriented Directed Acyclic Graph) toward a Root Node, and the routing header compression of RFC 8138, come from that concern.

Enabling RFC 8138 on a running network needs a flag day, where the network is upgraded and rebooted. Otherwise, a node without compression support acting as a leaf would fail to communicate, and acting as a router it would drop compressed packets and black-hole part of the network.

This document enables a hot upgrade instead. During migration compression stays inactive until all nodes are upgraded.
sections.eli5: Switching everyone to shorthand at once would be chaos if some kids had not learned it yet. This RFC lets the class switch only when everyone is ready.

sections.title: The T Flag in the DODAG Configuration Option
sections.content:
The DODAG Configuration option (Section 6.7.6 of RFC 6550) carries configuration for building and maintaining the DODAG. It was originally designed with four bit positions reserved for future flags. This document defines one: Enable Compression per RFC 8138 (T).

The T flag is set to turn on the use of RFC 8138 within the DODAG. It sits in position 2 of the reserved flags, counting from bit 0 as the most significant bit, and legacy implementations set it to 0.

The option is usually carried in a DIO message and copied unmodified from parents to children. RFC 6550 says nodes other than the DODAG root MUST NOT modify it, so even a legacy parent passes on the flag as the Root set it, and it floods transparently to every node.

For Mode of Operation (MOP) value 7, RFC 8138 MUST be used on links where 6LoWPAN Header Compression applies and MUST NOT be used otherwise. The flag definitions apply to MOP values 0 to 6 only.
sections.eli5: The flag is a little switch on a message that the boss at the top sends down. Everyone passes the message along without touching the switch.

sections.title: How Nodes Behave
sections.content:
A node SHOULD generate packets in compressed form using RFC 8138 if and only if the T flag is set. Configuration or network management can override this, for example to turn compression on when all nodes support it but the Root cannot set the flag, or to disable it locally in case of a problem.

The originator of a packet decides whether to compress, based on its capabilities and its knowledge of the flag. A router that encapsulates a packet is the originator of the new packet and compresses the outer headers, but it MUST NOT compress the encapsulated packet.

Routers forward a packet in the form the source used. The exception is a border router forwarding to an external target, which MUST uncompress the packet first, since an external target is not expected to support RFC 8138. An RPL-Unaware Leaf is both a leaf and an external target, so for it forwarding means delivering the packet.
sections.eli5: Whoever writes a note decides if it is in shorthand. Helpers pass it on as written, except when it goes to someone outside the class, who gets the long version.

sections.title: Transition Scenarios
sections.content:
A node that supports RFC 8138 but not this specification can only be used in a homogeneous network. The goal here is to migrate once and for all, without a flag day, and not to undo the setting of the T flag.

Coexistence. A node supporting this document works with compression on, off, or in transition. A node without RFC 8138 support can interoperate while compression is off. If it is on, a node that cannot handle compressed packets may stay connected as an RPL-Unaware Leaf.

Inconsistent state. When the Root turns the flag on, it percolates slowly as DIOs propagate, so some nodes start sending compressed packets while others do not know yet. All RPL nodes must support RFC 8138 at the time of the switch. Setting the flag is ultimately the network administrator's responsibility, and the network MUST be operated with the flag unset until all nodes in the RPL Instance are upgraded.

Rolling back. When turning compression off, the administrator MUST wait until each node has its flag unset before allowing nodes without compression support. Whether compression is active SHOULD be exposed in the node's management interface.
sections.eli5: The teacher only holds up the shorthand card when every kid has learned it. If shorthand is dropped later, the old-style kids wait until everyone has put the card down.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The document allocates one new flag in the IANA registry "DODAG Configuration Option Flags for MOP 0..6": bit number 2, "Enable Compression per RFC 8138 (T)", referencing RFC 9035. IANA also added this document as a reference for MOP 7 in the RPL "Mode of Operation" registry.
sections.eli5: The official list of flag switches got one new entry, so nobody else uses that spot for something different.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Any RPL-aware node with access to the RPL domain can inject RPL-based attacks (see RFC 7416). This document does not change those security requirements, and the new bit gets the same protection as the rest of the DODAG Configuration option.

Setting the flag before all routers are upgraded may cause packet loss. If the flag flips back and forth, both packet forms simply coexist at a cost of extra bandwidth for uncompressed packets, provided all nodes support RFC 8138.

An attacker could unset the flag to force extra energy use in its sub-DODAG, or set it so downstream nodes compress when they should not, potentially causing packet loss. Such attacks are more complex and more visible than simply dropping packets. A downstream node with other parents may see the bit with both settings, which can be detected and trigger an alert.
sections.eli5: A sneaky helper could flip the switch at the wrong time to waste batteries or lose notes, but that is easy to notice, especially if you hear from other helpers too.
